title: The shepherd boy's whistle
hookLine: a boy who couldn't read whistles in the synagogue on Yom Kippur, and the Baal Shem says it opened heaven

lines: EVERYONE KNOWS THE WORDS BUT YOU.
YOM KIPPUR, THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.
cards: Ever been in a room where everyone knew the words except you? A church, a temple, a stadium chant, a family song at a wedding. Everyone's singing, and you're moving your lips, hoping nobody notices.
Now a synagogue on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. The room is packed. People have fasted since yesterday.
The prayers are long and ancient and all in Hebrew. And in the back sits a village boy who can't read a single word. Hasidim tell this story in many versions.

teach.b: In one well-known telling, the boy is a shepherd who spends his days in the fields with the flock and has never learned to read. His father brings him to the synagogue of the Baal Shem Tov for Yom Kippur.
All day the boy watches everyone pray. He feels it; he wants to pray too. But he has no words.
In his pocket is the little whistle he uses in the fields.
Near the end of the day, in the closing prayer called Neilah, when the gates of heaven are said to be closing, he can't hold it in.
He pulls out the whistle and blows, loud and shrill, right in the middle of the holy silence. People are shocked. His father is mortified.
Some want to throw him out. But the Baal Shem Tov finishes the prayer with a shining face, and says: all day our prayers were stuck. They couldn't rise.
Then this boy's whistle, which came from the whole of his heart, broke through, and carried all our prayers up with it.
The story has no single written source; it's told in different versions, sometimes with a flute, sometimes about another rebbe.
But it rests on an old teaching from the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin: the Merciful One wants the heart.
What God wants most, the story says, isn't the right words. It's the whole heart, however it comes out.

how: Yom Kippur ends with Neilah, the closing prayer, and then a single long blast of the shofar; some Hasidic teachers tell this story before Neilah to encourage wholehearted prayer.

games.q: you're praying Neilah on Yom Kippur. a boy in the back suddenly blows a shepherd's whistle. what do you do?
o: throw him out for disrupting the prayer.
see it as a prayer from the whole heart.
games.why: the Baal Shem Tov said the prayers were stuck, and the boy's whistle, from the whole heart, carried them up.

practice: If you pray, you might have words you use, or none; if you don't, you might still have something you'd want to say to the world, or to life itself.
Forget the right words and find your whistle: a sigh, a hum, a thank you, a single honest sentence. Let it come from the whole of you, however plain it is.
